content: An if-sentence = condition + result.
ZERO: if + present, present.
If you press it, it stops.
(how things always work)
FIRST: if + present, will.
If they steal it, we will know.
(a real future set on a condition)
THE ONE RULE: the if-half never takes
'will'. Will lives in the result only.
Many languages use a special mood here;
English just reuses present and will.
SECOND conditional: if + past, would.
It is not about the past at all —
it paints an unreal NOW.
If I had it, I would give it to you.
(but I do not have it)
The past tense here is borrowed as a
distance-marker: one step from real.
IF I WERE YOU... is the advice frame.
Here 'were' stays for every person:
I, he, she — always 'were', not 'was'.
Would is the unreal-world helper.
Many languages use a special mood
for this; English borrows its past.
Reported speech folds someone's words
into your own sentence.
SAY or TELL + (that) + a sentence:
He said that he was innocent.
You SAY something; you TELL someone.
BACKSHIFT: the tense steps back one.
His words: 'I am innocent.'
Reported: he said he WAS innocent.
THAT is droppable — both are fine:
He said that he was late.
He said he was late.
Languages report speech differently;
English steps the tense back.
Sometimes the doer steps back, and the
thing acted on takes the subject seat.
That move is the passive.
Form: be + past participle.
"The suspect was arrested."           Press 1
"It is made in the factory."          Press 2
The doer can go unsaid, or ride at the
end in a by-phrase:
"...was arrested by the police."

pronunciation_mappings.2: It is made in the factory.

content: You will meet the passive most in news
and official writing:
"A new law was passed last week."
"The money has been found."
To read it: find the be-verb, then the
participle, and ask what the action
lands on. That thing is now the subject.
Many languages build the passive with a
special verb form or a small extra word.
English just reuses be - the same be you
have known since the very start.
A relative clause folds a full
description in behind its noun.
who = for people
which = for things
that = for people or things
"the woman who leads the team"
"the bird that sings at dawn"
"the law which was passed"
Reading skill: find the noun, bracket
the clause, and read on. A long sentence
is a short one wearing a description.
With the passive from Lesson 36, this is
the last door. These two make written
English look hard - and now you read
both with ease.
"the suspect who was arrested"
- a relative clause holding a passive.
Languages point the description in
different ways, and choose the joining
word by different rules. English keeps
it simple: pick who, which or that, and
the verb stays where it always sits.
Here is one sentence, built only from
grammar you now hold:
"The suspect who was arrested has been
set free, but if the police find new
proof, the trial will start again."
Clause by clause:
- who was arrested = a relative clause
- has been set free = present perfect,
in the passive
- if... will... = a first conditional
That is real written English, read
unaided.
You now hold the 1000 most frequent
English words, the full auxiliary system
- be, do, have, and the modals - and
both marked registers: the spoken
softeners and the written passive with
relative clauses.
At card one you needed to be and the
pronouns. You now read a line of real
text on your own.
P1 carries on by the same frequency law,
with the next 1000 words.
